title: The two jobs of probability and statistics
description: Statistics describes many cases by collecting and summarizing data; probability measures how likely things are.

facts.text: Statistics is the science of collecting, analyzing, interpreting and presenting data; organizing and summarizing data is called descriptive statistics.
Probability is the mathematics of chance: it deals with how likely an event is to happen.

title: John Graunt and London's Bills of Mortality
description: In 1662 John Graunt summed up London's weekly Bills of Mortality and found steady patterns, such as about 14 boys christened for every 13 girls.

facts.text: John Graunt, a London tradesman, published his Observations on London's Bills of Mortality in 1662, one of the first works of descriptive statistics.
London's Bills of Mortality were published every week and listed christenings, burials and causes of death, parish by parish.
Graunt found a steady ratio of about 14 boys christened for every 13 girls.

title: Pascal and Fermat's letters of 1654
description: In 1654 Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters on the problem of points, laying the foundation of probability theory.

facts.text: In letters exchanged in the summer of 1654, Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat laid the foundation of the theory of probability.
One puzzle Pascal and Fermat solved was the problem of points: how to split the stakes fairly when a game of chance stops before anyone has won.

title: Percent means per hundred
description: A percent is a ratio out of 100, from the Latin per centum, "by the hundred".

facts.text: The word percent comes from the Latin per centum, meaning "by the hundred".
A percent is a ratio out of 100, so 15% means 15 out of every 100; the same hundred appears in a century (100 years) and a cent (a hundredth of a dollar).

title: Turning "out of" into a percent
description: To turn a count out of a total into a percent, divide and move the decimal point two places right; percents put groups of different sizes on one scale.

facts.text: To turn a fraction into a percent, divide the top number by the bottom number, then move the decimal point two places to the right.
3 out of 20 is 15%: 3 ÷ 20 = 0.15, the same share as 15 out of 100 (scale both numbers up five times).
Percentages put groups of different sizes on one scale: 3 out of 20 (15%) is a bigger share than 12 out of 100 (12%).

title: Percent change
description: Percent change is the change (new minus old) divided by the starting value, written as a percent.

facts.text: Percent change is the amount of change (new minus old) divided by the starting amount, written as a percent.
A price rising from $20 to $25 has changed by $5, and 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, a 25% rise.

title: Percent change depends on the start
description: The same change is a big percent from a small start and a small percent from a big start.

facts.text: The same $5 rise on a $500 price, taking it to $505, is only a 1% increase, because 5 ÷ 500 = 0.01.
Because percent change divides by the starting value, the same amount of change is a bigger percent from a smaller start.
A price falling from $25 to $20 has fallen $5, and 5 ÷ 25 = 0.2, a 20% fall.

title: Up 50%, down 50%
description: An equal percent rise and fall do not cancel, because each percent is taken from a different starting value.

facts.text: $100 that falls 50% drops to $50; a 50% rise from $50 adds only $25, ending at $75, which is 25% below the start.
$100 that rises 50% becomes $150; a 50% fall from $150 removes $75, again ending at $75.
When a percent rise is followed by the same percent fall, or the reverse, the second percent is taken from a new value, so you end below the start: up 10% then down 10% turns $100 into $99.
After a 50% fall, it takes a 100% rise to get back to the start: from $50, regaining $50 is a change of 50 ÷ 50, or 100%.

title: Percent vs. percentage points
description: The difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points; percent change compares that difference with the starting value.

facts.text: The plain difference between two percentages is measured in percentage points; a percent change instead divides the change by the starting value.
A share rising from 10% to 15% has risen 5 percentage points, which is a 50 percent increase, since 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5: 10 in every 100 became 15 in every 100.

Jennifer LaFleur, an editor quoted by The Journalist's Resource, warns that percent change and percentage-point change "get mixed up all the time"; when comparing two percentages, the difference is in percentage points.

title: Rates: counting per person
description: Totals mislead when places differ in size; a rate divides the count by the population, often per 100,000 people.

facts.text: Counts don't take a population's size into account, so they can't fairly compare how often something happens in places of different sizes.
A rate divides a count by the size of the population and is often scaled to a round number of people, such as per 100,000.
A town of 10,000 people with 50 cases has a rate of 500 per 100,000; a city of 1,000,000 with 500 cases has 10 times the cases but a rate of 50 per 100,000, a tenth of the town's.
Because a rate puts a count in the perspective of the population, it is a measure of how common something is for each person; a percent is simply a rate per 100.

title: Switching between percents and "1 in N"
description: "1 in N" is 100 divided by N percent; a bigger N means a smaller share, which famously confused buyers of a third-pound burger.

facts.text: In the 1980s A&W sold a third-pound burger for the same price as McDonald's Quarter Pounder; according to owner A. Alfred Taubman, focus groups showed many people thought a third of a pound was smaller than a quarter.
1 in 4 is one quarter, or 25%; 1 in 5 is 20%; 1 in 3 is about 33%. Dividing 100 by N turns "1 in N" into a percent, and dividing 100 by the percent turns it back.
In "1 in N", a bigger N means a smaller share: 1 in 3 (a third) is more than 1 in 4 (a quarter).

title: Counts of people are easier to picture
description: Many people grasp simple counts like "2 in 5" better than percentages, and counts with the same bottom number are easiest to compare.

facts.text: Some data suggest patients understand simple counts, such as 2 in 5, better than percentages, such as 40 percent.
Risk communicators advise comparing counts with the same bottom number, such as about 4 in 50 against 3 in 50, rather than 1 in 12 against 1 in 17.
Risk experts warn that the "1 in X" format can make a risk seem bigger than it is.

title: Thousand, million, billion
description: Each step from thousand to million to billion multiplies by 1,000, as the SI prefixes kilo, mega and giga do.

facts.text: A thousand is 1,000; a million is 1,000 thousands (1,000,000); a billion is 1,000 millions (1,000,000,000). The SI prefixes kilo, mega and giga stand for thousand, million and billion.

title: A billion seconds
description: Counted in seconds, a million is about 11 and a half days while a billion is almost 32 years.

facts.text: A day has 86,400 seconds.
1,000 seconds is about 17 minutes, 1 million seconds is about 11 and a half days, 1 billion seconds is almost 32 years, and 1 trillion seconds is about 31,700 years.

title: Wunderlich's 98.6°F
description: The 98.6°F standard comes from Carl Wunderlich's 1868 average of 37°C, converted to Fahrenheit.

facts.text: In his 1868 book, Carl Wunderlich reportedly analyzed over a million underarm temperature readings from some 25,000 patients, and gave 37°C (98.6°F) as healthy adults' average.
To convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 1.8 and add 32, so 37°C is exactly 98.6°F.
NIST's table of everyday temperatures lists body temperature as 37°C and 99°F.

title: Too precise to be true
description: A number can look more exact than the measurement behind it; converting a round figure adds decimals without adding precision.

facts.text: A result calculated from a measurement is at least as uncertain as the measurement itself, so converting a number cannot make it more precise.
A temperature given to the nearest whole degree, like 37°C, could be anything from 36.5°C to 37.5°C, which is 97.7°F to 99.5°F.

title: Measuring body temperature again in 1992
description: A 1992 study of 148 healthy adults found an average of 98.2°F, and exactly 98.6°F in only 8% of readings.

facts.text: In a 1992 study, University of Maryland researchers took 700 oral readings from 148 healthy adults; the average was 36.8°C (98.2°F), and 37°C (98.6°F) came up in only 56 of the 700 readings, or 8%.

title: Every share hides an "out of what"
description: Percents, percent changes, rates and "1 in N" counts all compare a part with a whole, so the first question for any of them is: out of what?

facts.text: Percents, percent changes, rates and "1 in N" counts all compare a part with a whole: out of 100, out of the starting value, out of the population or out of N.

title: The mean: add up and share out
description: The mean adds up every value and divides by how many there are: the fair share each would get if the total were split equally.

facts.text: The mean, or arithmetic average, is the sum of all the values in a data set divided by the number of values.
Five bottles holding 1, 4, 2, 3 and 0 liters of water hold 10 liters in all; shared equally, each gets 10 ÷ 5 = 2 liters, which is the mean.
The mean can be thought of as a fair share, or leveling out: the amount each member of a group would have if all the values were combined and shared out equally.
Quiz scores of 70, 90, 86 and 94 add up to 340, and 340 ÷ 4 = 85, so the mean is 85, although no single quiz scored 85.
The words "mean" and "average" are often used interchangeably; the mean is the most common measure of the center, and because it includes every value, outliers influence it.
Per capita income is a mean: all the income of the people in a place added up and divided by its total population, every man, woman and child.

title: The median: the middle one
description: The median is the middle value once the data are in order, with half the values on each side; for an even count it is halfway between the two middle values.

facts.text: The median is the middle value once the values are put in order; it divides the data in half, with 50% of the values on either side.
The retirement ages of 11 people, lined up from 54 to 60 (54, 54, 54, 55, 56, 57, 57, 58, 58, 60, 60), have a median of 57: the sixth value, with five ages on each side.
With an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values: adding a retirement age of 52 makes 12 values, whose two middle ages are 56 and 57, so the median is 56.5.
For the 11 retirement ages, the ages add up to 623 and the mean is 623 ÷ 11, about 56.6 years, close to the median of 57.

title: When mean and median disagree
description: A few very large values pull the mean far above the median, as with incomes: the mean counts every value, the median only the middle.

facts.text: If nine people earn $50,000 and a tenth earns $1,050,000, the total is $1,500,000, so the mean is $150,000, three times what nine of them earn, while the median stays $50,000.
Because the mean includes every value, outliers and lopsided data pull it; the median, which depends only on the middle of the ordered list, is much less affected.
When data have a long tail of high values (skewed to the right), the mean is usually pulled toward the tail, and most values, including the median, sit below the mean.
A handful of very high values, such as top incomes or one mansion among ordinary homes, lift the mean much more than the median, so the median is usually preferred for lopsided data.
In 2024, US median household income was $83,730 and mean household income was $121,000, about $37,000 higher.
The Census Bureau defines median income as the amount that divides households into two equal groups: half have incomes above the median and half below.

title: The mode: most popular wins
description: The mode is the most common value. It is the only average that works for categories, a set can have several modes or none, and it may sit away from the center.

facts.text: The mode is the value that occurs most often in a set of data.
For shoe sizes 6, 7, 7, 7 and 11, the mode is 7, worn by three of the five; the mean is 38 ÷ 5 = 7.6, a size nobody in the group wears.
The mode works for categories as well as numbers: for red, red, red, green, green, yellow, purple, black, blue, the mode is red, while a mean or median cannot be found for colors.
A data set can have two modes (bimodal) or more, or none if every value is different, and the mode may sit away from the center: for the 11 retirement ages the mode is 54, while the middle is 57.

title: Outliers: fix or keep
description: An outlier is a value far from the rest. Investigate it: a proven mistake is corrected or removed; a real value is kept, and may be the most interesting one.

facts.text: Outliers are extreme values notably different from the rest of the data; they can change the results of an analysis, so a potential outlier always needs further investigation.
Changing one retirement age from 60 to 81 in the list of 11 raises the mean from about 56.6 to about 58.5 years (644 ÷ 11), but the median stays 57.
An outlier may be bad data, such as a value recorded incorrectly or an experiment not run correctly; if it is shown to be an error, it should be corrected if possible or removed.
A child's age entered as 123 in a survey of schoolchildren is an impossible value, so it must be a recording mistake.
An outlier may also be a real value, from random variation or something genuinely interesting, so outliers should not simply be deleted.
Robert Wadlow, measured at 272 cm (8 ft 11.1 in) in 1940, is the tallest man in medical history for whom there is irrefutable evidence.

title: Same average, different spread: the range
description: Two sets can share an average and still differ in how spread out they are. The range, largest minus smallest, is the simplest measure, but it uses only two values.

facts.text: Exam scores of 40, 70 and 100 and scores of 69, 70 and 71 both have a mean of 70; in the first set one score is 30 below the mean and one 30 above, while the second is tightly clustered.
Two data sets can have the same average yet very different spread, so reporting the mean alone is often not enough; a measure of spread is needed too.
The range is the largest value minus the smallest: 100 − 40 = 60 points for the first set of exam scores, and 71 − 69 = 2 points for the second.
The range uses only two values, the largest and the smallest, so it ignores everything in between and a single outlier at either end can stretch it.

title: The standard deviation in plain words
description: The standard deviation is a typical distance of values from their mean, built from every value: small when values bunch together, large when they scatter.

facts.text: The standard deviation measures how far data values are from their mean, using how close each value is to the mean; it is in the same units as the data and shows whether a value is close to or far from the mean.

A small standard deviation means values sit close to the mean, and if all values are equal it is zero: two data sets with a mean of 6, one running from 4 to 8 (mostly 5s, 6s and 7s) and one from 1 to 11, have standard deviations of about 1 and about 3.
Karl Pearson introduced the term "standard deviation" in a lecture in 1893 and in print in 1894, replacing older names such as "mean error"; the idea itself was nearly a century old.

title: The bell curve
description: In a bell curve most values bunch near the middle and thin out evenly on both sides; about 68% lie within one standard deviation of the mean and about 95% within two.

facts.text: In 1846 the Belgian scholar Adolphe Quetelet used records of the chest sizes of 5,738 Scottish militiamen to show that human measurements follow the bell-shaped normal curve.
In Quetelet's data the most common chest sizes were 39 and 40 inches, with more than 1,000 men each (1,073 and 1,079), and the counts fell away steadily toward the extremes of 33 and 48 inches.
A bell-shaped normal distribution is symmetrical, so its mean, median and mode all sit together in the middle.
Many measurements come close to a bell curve, such as heights within one sex and most IQ scores, but the normal distribution cannot be applied to everything.
In a normal distribution, about 68% of values (roughly two-thirds) lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two and about 99.7% within three.
In a textbook example, 15- to 18-year-old boys in Chile in 2009 to 2010 had a mean height of 170 cm with a standard deviation of about 6 cm, so about 68% were roughly 164 to 176 cm tall.

title: Percentiles
description: A percentile gives a value's place in ordered data: at the 90th percentile, 90% of values are the same or lower. Growth charts compare a child with others of the same sex and age.

facts.text: Percentiles divide ordered data into hundredths: scoring in the 90th percentile on an exam means 90% of scores were the same as or below yours, not that you got 90% right.
On CDC growth charts, a 5-year-old girl at the 25th percentile for weight weighs the same as or more than 25% of 5-year-old girls in the reference population, and less than 75%.
Growth charts compare a child with children of the same sex and age; the CDC 2000 growth charts were built from national surveys that measured US children.
The median is the 50th percentile; the 25th and 75th percentiles are called the lower and upper quartiles.

title: Describe data with a center and a spread
description: One number for the middle and one for the spread describe a data set far better than either alone: pick the average that fits, then say how scattered the values are.

facts.text: Measures of the center and measures of spread are used together: the center gives a typical value, and the spread shows how scattered the values are around it.

title: The probability scale from 0 to 1
description: Every probability lies between 0 (the event never happens) and 1 (it always happens); 0.5 means as likely as not, which is 50% or 1 in 2.

facts.text: Probabilities lie between 0 and 1: 0 means the event never happens, 1 means it always happens, and 0.5 (50%, or 1 in 2) means it is as likely to happen as not.
A fair six-sided die has the faces 1 to 6, each as likely as any other, so rolling a 7 with one die is impossible.

title: Probability as a long-run share
description: The probability of an outcome is its long-term relative frequency: the share of times it happens over very many tries, not a prediction for one try.

facts.text: The probability of an outcome is its long-term relative frequency: flip a fair coin 20, then 2,000, then 20,000 times and the share of heads approaches 0.5.

title: Counting equally likely outcomes
description: When outcomes are equally likely, a probability is the number of outcomes you want divided by the total number of outcomes.

facts.text: When all outcomes are equally likely, the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in it divided by the total: rolling at least 5 on a fair die is 2 outcomes (5 and 6) out of 6.

title: Galileo's three dice
description: Dice players found three dice total 10 more often than 9; Galileo explained it by counting all 216 throws: 27 make 10 and only 25 make 9.

facts.text: Dice players had found by long observation that three dice total 10 more often than 9, although each total can be made from six sets of numbers; Galileo was asked to explain why.
Galileo counted throws, not sums: two dice give 6 × 6 = 36 throws and three give 216; of the 216, a total of 10 comes up in 27 throws and 9 in only 25.

title: The 36 throws of two dice
description: Two dice, told apart, give 36 equally likely throws; 7 can be made six ways (1 in 6), while 2 and 12 can each be made only one way (1 in 36).

facts.text: Two dice give 36 equally likely throws when you tell them apart (imagine one red and one blue), so a red 2 with a blue 5 is a different throw from a red 5 with a blue 2.

A total of 7 can be made six ways out of 36 (1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, each either way round), so its chance is 1 in 6, the highest of any total; 2 (snake eyes, both dice on 1) and 12 (double 6) each have a chance of 1 in 36.

title: Multiplying independent chances
description: For independent events, the chance that both happen is the product of their chances: two sixes is 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36, and each extra coin flip halves the chance of an all-heads run.

facts.text: When two events are independent, the chance that both happen is their two chances multiplied together.
The chance of two sixes on two fair dice is 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36, the same as the one throw out of 36 that shows double 6.
For a fair coin, two heads in a row has a chance of 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, three in a row 1/8, and ten in a row 1/2 multiplied 10 times, or 1 in 1,024.

title: With and without replacement
description: Drawing cards and putting each back keeps the draws independent; keeping them out changes the deck, so the first draw changes the chances for the second.

facts.text: Picking with replacement (putting each card back) keeps picks independent; picking without replacement makes them dependent, because the first pick changes the chances for the second.
A standard deck has 52 cards in four suits of 13, so a heart is 1 in 4; with replacement, two hearts is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16, but after keeping one heart out, only 12 hearts remain among 51 cards.

title: The chance of at least one
description: An event and its opposite have chances that add up to 1, so the chance of "at least one" is 1 minus the chance of none.

facts.text: An event and its complement (everything else that can happen) have chances that add up to 1, so if a six has a chance of 1/6, no six has a chance of 5/6.
The chance of at least one success is 1 minus the chance of no successes at all, which for independent tries can be found by multiplying.

title: De Méré's dice bets
description: At least one six in four rolls of a die comes up about 52% of the time; at least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice only about 49%.

facts.text: The Chevalier de Méré, a French gambler, suspected that betting on at least one six in four rolls of a die was a good bet, and posed the question to Pascal, who proved him right.
No six in four rolls of a fair die has a chance of 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6 = 625/1,296, about 48%, so at least one six comes up 671 times in 1,296, about 52%.
At least one double 6 in 24 rolls of two dice has a chance of about 49% (no double 6 on a roll is 35/36, multiplied 24 times), just under even and below the four-roll bet.

title: Independent events have no memory
description: Events are independent when one happening does not change the chance of the other; coin flips and die rolls are independent, so a coin that landed heads five times is still 50/50.

facts.text: Two events are independent if knowing that one happened does not change the chance of the other; the results of two rolls of a fair die are independent.
Coin flips are independent, so after five heads in a row, a fair coin still has a 1 in 2 chance of heads on the next flip.
The law of averages does not say that after a run of heads, a head becomes less likely: every flip starts afresh.

title: Every sequence is equally likely
description: Before any flips, six heads in a row is rare (1 in 64), but so is every other particular sequence of six flips; once five heads have landed, only one 50/50 flip is left.

facts.text: Every particular sequence of flips of a fair coin is equally likely: HHHHHH and HHHHHT each have a chance of 1 in 64 before you start, but once five heads have landed, the last flip is 50/50.

title: The gambler's fallacy
description: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that after a long streak of one outcome, a different outcome has become more likely; for independent events, the chances stay the same.

facts.text: The gambler's fallacy is the belief that after a long streak of one outcome, a different outcome has become more likely.
Roulette spins are independent: the chance of red on any spin is the same whatever came before, so after 26 blacks the chance of red on spin 27 was unchanged.

title: Monte Carlo, 1913
description: On 18 August 1913, a roulette ball at the Monte Carlo casino fell on black 26 times in a row; gamblers bet ever more on red and lost millions.

facts.text: On 18 August 1913, at the casino in Monte Carlo, the roulette ball fell on black 26 times in a row; as the streak grew, gamblers shifted their bets to red, feeling red was due, and lost millions.

title: Randomness is streaky
description: Real random sequences contain longer streaks than people expect: in 200 coin tosses the longest run is typically about eight, while invented lists rarely pass five.

facts.text: In a classroom test, half the students toss a coin 200 times and half invent 200 tosses; statistician Mark Schilling sorted them correctly about 85% of the time, because the invented lists had streaks that were too short.
In 200 real tosses of a fair coin, the longest run of all heads or all tails is typically about eight; very few students inventing 200 tosses write a run longer than five.

Any one long run is rare, but 200 flips give a run many places to start, so a run of several heads in a row is almost bound to appear: the longest run of heads in 200 tosses falls between 4 and 10 about 95% of the time.

title: The hot hand debate
description: A famous 1985 study called basketball's hot hand an illusion; in 2018 Miller and Sanjurjo found a bias in its method, and correcting it reversed the conclusion. The debate continues.

facts.text: The "hot hand" is the belief that a basketball player who has just made shots is more likely to make the next one; a famous 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky concluded the belief was an illusion.

In 2018, economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo showed that the 1985 study counted streaks in a subtly biased way; correcting the bias reversed its conclusion, though whether fans overrate the hot hand is still open.

title: The law of large numbers
description: As tries pile up, the share of an outcome settles close to its true chance; over a few tries it swings widely. Early luck is swamped, not repaid.

facts.text: The law of large numbers says that as the number of tries grows, the share of times an outcome happens gets closer and closer to its true chance; it was first proved by Jakob Bernoulli in 1713.
The chance of getting between 40% and 60% heads is about 66% for 10 tosses of a fair coin (4 to 6 heads), 96% for 100 tosses, and almost 100% for 1,000 tosses.

The count of heads minus half the tosses does not shrink toward zero as tosses pile up, but that gap divided by the number of tosses does: an early shortfall, like 3 heads in the first 10, is swamped after 1,000 tosses rather than paid back.

title: Kerrich's 10,000 coin tosses
description: Held in a prison camp in Denmark during World War II, John Kerrich tossed a coin 10,000 times and got 5,067 heads, about 50.7%.

facts.text: John Kerrich, an English mathematician held in a prison camp in Denmark during World War II, tossed a coin 10,000 times and got 5,067 heads, a share of about 50.7% and 67 more than an even 5,000.

title: The birthday problem
description: With 23 people, the chance that two share a birthday is 50.7%, found by multiplying the chances that each new person misses everyone before; with 57 people it is about 99%.

facts.text: In a group of 23 people, the chance that at least two share a birthday is 50.7%, just better than even.

The chance that nobody shares a birthday is found by multiplying: the second person misses the first 364 times in 365, the third misses both 363 times in 365, and so on; by the 23rd person it has fallen just below half.
With 57 people, the chance of a shared birthday is about 99%; the calculation assumes birthdays are spread evenly over 365 days and leaves out leap years, which makes a negligible difference.

title: Count pairs, not people
description: The birthday problem asks about any two people, not you: 23 people make 253 pairs, each a chance for a match, and pairs grow much faster than people.

facts.text: The birthday problem asks whether any two people match, not whether someone matches you: 23 people make 22 + 21 + ... + 1 = 253 different pairs.
Pairs grow much faster than people: 23 people make 253 pairs, while 57 people make 1,596.

title: Chance's three tools
description: Most chance questions yield to three tools: count equally likely outcomes, multiply the chances of independent events, and for "at least one", take the chance of none from 1.

facts.text: Three tools answer most simple chance questions: count equally likely outcomes and divide; multiply the chances of independent events; and for "at least one", subtract the chance of none from 1.

title: What odds compare
description: Odds compare the chances against an event with the chances for it; probability compares the chances for it with the whole.

facts.text: Odds compare the chance of success with the chance of failure, while a probability compares success with all the outcomes.
A standard deck has 52 cards in four suits of 13 cards each; hearts are one of the four suits.
Drawing one card, 13 of the 52 cards are hearts and 39 are not, so the odds are 39 to 13, or 3 to 1, against a heart, and the chance is 13 in 52, or 1 in 4.

title: Switching between odds and probability
description: To turn odds into a probability, add the two numbers to get the whole; to go back, split the whole into wins and losses.

facts.text: Odds of 3 to 1 against mean 3 ways to lose and 1 to win, 4 in all, so the chance of winning is 1 in 4, or 25%: add the two numbers to find the whole.
A 1 in 5 chance is 1 win to 4 losses, or 4 to 1 against; an 80% chance is 80 to 20, or 4 to 1 in favor; a 50% chance is 1 to 1.

title: Expected value
description: A bet's expected value is its average result per play over many plays: multiply each outcome by its chance and add.

facts.text: Expected value is the long-term average result: multiply each possible outcome by its probability, then add the results.
In a coin game paying $3 for heads and costing $2 for tails, each weighed by one half, the expected value is $1.50 minus $1, or 50 cents a flip.
Expected value is an average over many plays, and real results vary around it: at 50 cents a flip, 100 flips would be expected to come out about $50 ahead.
In a textbook game you pay $2 for a 1 in 100,000 chance at $100,000; the prize weighed by its chance is worth $1, so you lose about $1 a play on average.

title: The house edge in roulette
description: American roulette pays single-number bets as if the wheel had 36 pockets, not 38; the gap is a house edge of about 5.26% of every bet.

facts.text: An American roulette wheel has 38 pockets: 1 to 36 in red and black, plus a green 0 and 00.
A bet on a single number in roulette pays 35 to 1.
With 1 winning pocket and 37 losing ones, the true odds against a single number are 37 to 1; a 35 to 1 payout would be fair only on a wheel of 36 pockets.
Betting $1 on one number for 38 spins and winning once returns $36 ($35 plus the $1 stake) for $38 staked: a $2 loss, 2 parts in 38, or about 5.26%.
The house edge is about 5.26% on almost every bet on an American double-zero wheel and about 2.7% on a single-zero European wheel.
Because expected value is the long-term average, over many bets the casino keeps close to 5.26 cents of every dollar wagered on the American wheel.

title: The odds of a lottery jackpot
description: A $2 Powerball play has a 1 in 292,201,338 chance at the jackpot, far less likely than being struck by lightning in a given year.

facts.text: A Powerball play costs $2: pick 5 numbers from 1 to 69 and a Powerball from 1 to 26. The odds of matching all six for the jackpot are 1 in 292,201,338.
292,201,338 seconds (about 292 million) is more than 9 years, at 86,400 seconds a day.
Based on 2009 to 2018 averages, the National Weather Service puts the odds of being struck by lightning in a given year at 1 in 1,222,000.
292,201,338 divided by 1,222,000 is about 239, so a year's chance of a lightning strike is more than 200 times the chance of one ticket winning the jackpot.

title: A lottery ticket's expected value
description: About half of every dollar played in Powerball goes to prizes, so on average a $2 play returns about $1: its expected value is below its price.

facts.text: About 50% of each dollar played in Powerball is allocated to prizes, so across all tickets a $2 play returns about $1 in prizes on average.
The overall odds of winning any Powerball prize are 1 in 24.87 (about 1 in 25), and the smallest prizes are $4 and $7.

title: Insurance as a bet
description: Insurance premiums must cover claims, running costs and profit, so the average buyer pays in more than they get back: a negative expected value.

facts.text: Insurance is a pool: members pay regular premiums, and those who suffer a covered loss are paid from it, so no single event hits them too hard.
Over time, the average person's premiums must cover the average claims, the costs of running the company and its profit, so the average buyer pays in more than they get back.
With a $1,000 bike and a 1 in 100 (1 percent) yearly chance of replacing it, the expected loss is $10 a year; an insurer charges that $10 plus a little extra.

title: Paying to avoid a gamble
description: Risk-averse people will pay more than a gamble's expected loss to avoid it, and prefer a sure thing to a gamble with the same expected value.

facts.text: Economists call people risk-averse when they are willing to pay more than a gamble's expected loss to avoid it, and most people are; risk aversion lets insurers make money.
Risk-averse people prefer a sure thing to a gamble that has the same expected value.

title: The Monty Hall puzzle
description: When a host who knows where the car is opens a goat door, switching wins 2 times in 3, because your first pick was a goat 2 times in 3.

facts.text: In 1990 columnist Marilyn vos Savant explained in Parade magazine that you should switch, drawing thousands of letters, many from academics, insisting she was wrong.
The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the game show Let's Make a Deal. The host knows where the car is and opens an unchosen door that hides a goat.
Switching wins 2 times in 3 and staying wins 1 time in 3: your first pick is a goat 2 times in 3, and then the only other closed door hides the car.
Your first door has a 1 in 3 chance and the other two doors together 2 in 3; when the host opens a goat door among them, that whole 2 in 3 rests on the door left shut.
Winning 2 times in 3 means 2 wins to 1 loss: odds of 2 to 1 in favor of switching.

title: Expected value for an everyday choice
description: Compare a sure cost with the expected cost of a gamble, and find the break-even chance where they are equal.

facts.text: In an example with made-up round numbers, a parking meter costs $4, the fine for not paying is $50, and the chance of a ticket is 1 in 5.
At a 1 in 5 chance, a $50 fine has an expected cost of $10, against a sure $4, so paying saves $6 on average; at 1 in 10 the expected fine is $5, still above $4.
The two choices cost the same on average when the chance times $50 equals $4: a chance of 4 in 50, or 8 in 100.
An expected value includes only the outcomes and amounts put into it; any cost left out of the calculation cannot show up in the result.

title: Same average, different risk
description: Two bets can share an expected value yet differ in how far apart their outcomes are and how bad the worst one is.

facts.text: A sure $50 and a coin flip for $100 or nothing both have an expected value of $50.
On a single play you get one of the actual outcomes, never the average: a flip for $100 or nothing pays $100 or $0, not $50.
A coin bet to win or lose $1 and one to win or lose $1,000 both have an expected value of $0, but the second can cost $1,000 on one flip.

title: Monte Carlo simulation
description: Estimate a chance too hard to calculate by running many random pretend trials and counting the share that succeed; Ulam had the idea in 1946.

facts.text: In 1946, recovering from an illness, Stanislaw Ulam asked how likely a solitaire hand of 52 cards was to come out; working it out exactly was monstrously difficult.
Ulam's idea was to lay the cards out a hundred times and count the successful games, each starting from a random shuffle, instead of calculating.
As the number of trials grows, the observed share of successes tends to get closer to the true probability.

Ulam and John von Neumann applied the idea to neutron problems at Los Alamos; Nick Metropolis named it Monte Carlo, after the casino town Ulam's uncle borrowed money to visit. It first ran on ENIAC in 1948.
The mathematician Paul Erdős reportedly doubted the Monty Hall answer until computer simulations confirmed it.
In 3,000 simulated Monty Hall games with a player who always switches, about 2,000 wins are expected, since 2 in 3 of 3,000 is 2,000.
Monte Carlo methods are now used across science, finance, transport, health and manufacturing, wherever risks must be measured.

title: Three questions for any bet
description: Judge a bet by its chance (turn odds into a probability), its expected value (weigh each outcome by its chance) and its worst case.

facts.text: To judge a bet, turn its odds into a probability, weigh each outcome by its chance to get the expected value, and check how bad the worst outcome could be.

title: Absolute risk
description: Absolute risk is the plain chance that something happens to people in a group over a set time: how many, out of how many, over how long.

facts.text: Absolute risk is the chance that something will happen to a person in a group over a certain period of time.
In a shuffled 52-card deck, the absolute risk of drawing any heart is 1 in 4 (25%); the risk of drawing the queen of diamonds is 1 in 52, just under 2%.
An absolute risk needs a time period: the chance of something happening over one year is different from the chance over a lifetime.
A risk of 2 in 1,000 over 10 years is 0.2%: 2 ÷ 1,000 = 0.002.
A relative risk says how much more or less likely something is in one group than another, but on its own it says nothing about how likely it is at all.

title: Relative risk
description: Relative risk compares the risk in two groups. "Doubles your risk" can mean 1 in 10,000 becoming 2 in 10,000, so ask for the absolute risks before and after.

facts.text: Relative risk compares the risk of an event in one group with the risk in another group; a relative risk of 1 means no difference, and above 1 means a higher risk.
A risk that rises from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000 has doubled (a relative risk of 2), yet it adds only 1 extra case per 10,000 people.
A risk that rises from 1 in 10 to 2 in 10 has also doubled, but that is 1,000 extra cases per 10,000 people.
A 2012 study of more than 175,000 young people found that repeated CT scans in childhood could triple the risk of leukemia and brain tumors.
The same study estimated about one extra case of leukemia and one extra brain tumor for every 10,000 head CT scans in children aged 10 or under, over the following 10 years.
The researchers stressed that when a child needs a CT scan, its benefits should outweigh the small future cancer risk.
When the starting risk is very small, even a large relative increase makes little absolute difference; when the starting risk is large, a small relative increase can affect many people.

title: Number needed to treat
description: The number needed to treat is how many people take a treatment over a set time for one to benefit; it is 100 divided by the drop in absolute risk in percentage points.

facts.text: If a treatment cuts the 2-year risk of a heart attack from 2% on placebo to 1%, that is a 50% relative reduction but only 1 percentage point of absolute risk, so 100 people must be treated for 2 years to prevent one heart attack.
The number needed to treat is how many people must receive a treatment over a set time for one of them to benefit, such as avoiding one heart attack.
The number needed to treat first appeared in the medical literature in 1988.
To find the number needed to treat, divide 100 by the drop in absolute risk in percentage points: a drop from 10% to 5% gives 100 ÷ 5 = 20.
A treatment that helps everyone has a number needed to treat of 1; one that helps half has 2; one that helps a quarter has 4, like a 25% free-throw shooter needing about 4 tries per basket.
In the 2%-to-1% example, of 100 people treated, about 98 would not have had a heart attack anyway, about 1 has one despite treatment, and about 1 is spared.

title: Risk per mile, per hour or per trip
description: Comparing travel risks depends on the rate's "per": per mile flying is far safer than driving, but per trip the gap narrows because crashes cluster at takeoff and landing.

facts.text: In 2023 US figures, people in cars and trucks died at more than 100 times the airline passengers' rate per mile traveled: 0.53 against 0.003 deaths per 100 million passenger miles.
Most fatal airliner accidents happen around takeoff and landing rather than in the long cruise between: of those from 2004 to 2013, only about 1 in 10 happened in cruise.
Counted per journey instead of per mile, analyses of 1990s data found flying riskier than a car trip.
Travel risk can be measured per distance, per hour or per journey, and which way of traveling looks safest changes with the choice.

title: Base rates
description: The base rate (prevalence) is how common something is in the whole population; start from it before judging a single case, as in "think horses, not zebras".

facts.text: The medical saying "When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras" is usually credited to Theodore Woodward of the University of Maryland School of Medicine, who reportedly used a version of it from the 1940s.
The saying reminds doctors that a common explanation is far more likely than a rare one; "zebra" became medical slang for a surprising, rare diagnosis.
How common something is in a whole population, the share of people who have it, is called its prevalence or base rate; it can be given as a percent or per 10,000 or 100,000 people.
In a made-up town of 10,000 people where 1,000 have a cold and 1 has a rare illness, and both cause a cough, colds outnumber the rare illness 1,000 to 1 among people with a cough.
Test results and other clues should be read in the context of how common a condition is in the population.

title: Sensitivity and specificity
description: Sensitivity is how many people with a condition a test catches; specificity is how many people without it the test clears. Moving the cutoff trades one against the other.

facts.text: A test result can be a true positive, a false positive, a true negative or a false negative.
Sensitivity is how well a test identifies people who do have a condition: 90% sensitivity detects 90 of every 100 such people.
Specificity is how well a test identifies people who do not have a condition: 90% specificity correctly clears 90 of every 100 such people.
At 90% sensitivity, 10 of every 100 people with the condition are missed (false negatives); at 90% specificity, 10 of every 100 without it get a false alarm (false positives).
Moving a test's cutoff trades one measure against the other: a cutoff that catches more true cases also flags more healthy people, raising sensitivity but lowering specificity.

title: Why most positives can be false
description: Counting 10,000 people through a good test for a rare condition shows that false alarms from the many healthy people can outnumber the true cases.

facts.text: In a made-up group of 10,000 people where 1% have a condition, 100 people have it and 9,900 do not; a test with 90% sensitivity catches 90 of the 100 and misses 10.
Of the 9,900 people without the condition, a test with 90% specificity clears 8,910 and wrongly flags the other 10%: 990 false alarms.
That gives 1,080 positive results, of which only 90 are real: 1 in 12.
The share of positive results that are real (the positive predictive value) rises as a condition becomes more common in the group tested.
If 1 in 10 of the 10,000 people had the condition, the same test would give 900 true and 900 false positives, so 1 in 2 positives would be real.
Most positives from a test for a rare condition can be false because people without it vastly outnumber people with it, so even a small share of them outnumbers the true cases.

title: Bayes' idea: updating from the base rate
description: Bayes' idea in words: start from the base rate and let each piece of evidence shift the chance up or down by the right amount.

facts.text: Thomas Bayes, an English minister, died in 1761; his friend Richard Price found an essay on probability among his papers and sent it to the Royal Society, which published it.
Bayes' rule combines a starting probability, such as a base rate, with new evidence to give an updated probability, which can then be the starting point for the next piece of evidence.

In Level 47's example, if the 1,080 people who tested positive take a second test of the same quality whose mistakes are unrelated to the first, 81 of the 90 sick and 99 of the 990 healthy test positive again: 81 of 180, or 45%, are real.
Doctors often follow a positive screening test with a second, more specific test before concluding that someone has a disease.
In the same example, a negative first test leaves 10 sick people among 8,920 negatives, cutting the chance from 1 in 100 to about 1 in 900.

title: The prosecutor's fallacy and the Sally Clark case
description: A tiny chance of the evidence arising innocently is not the chance of innocence; the 1 in 73 million figure in the Sally Clark case was both invalid and misread.

facts.text: Sally Clark, an English solicitor, was convicted in November 1999 of murdering her two baby sons.

At her trial, a medical expert witness told the jury that the chance of two cot deaths (sudden infant death syndrome) in a family like hers was 1 in 73 million, a figure he got by squaring the chance of one.
Squaring is valid only if cot deaths strike independently within families; unknown genetic or environmental factors may make a second cot death in the same family much more likely.
The Royal Statistical Society said in October 2001 that the 1 in 73 million figure had no statistical basis.
Some press reports called 1 in 73 million the chance that the deaths were accidental; the Royal Statistical Society called this error the prosecutor's fallacy.

The jury needed to weigh two competing explanations, cot death or murder, each very unlikely; what matters is how likely the deaths are under each explanation compared with the other, not how unlikely they are under one.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission found the medical and statistical evidence at trial misleading and important bacteriological evidence undisclosed; the Court of Appeal quashed her convictions in January 2003.

title: Taking apart a risk claim
description: To judge a risk claim, ask for absolute risks behind relative ones, what the rate is counted per, the base rate, and how many positive results are real.

facts.text: To judge a risk claim, ask for the absolute risks behind any relative risk, and for the base rate behind any test result.

title: Population and sample
description: The population is the whole group you want to know about; a sample is the portion you actually examine, because checking everyone costs too much time and money.

facts.text: A population is the whole group being studied; a sample is a portion of it, selected and studied to learn about the population.
Examining a whole population takes a lot of time and money and is often impossible, so studying a sample is a practical technique.
In presidential elections, opinion polls take samples of 1,000 to 2,000 people to represent the views of the whole country.

title: A sample's statistic estimates the population's parameter
description: A number worked out from a sample (a statistic) estimates the matching number for the whole population (a parameter); how well depends on how representative the sample is, and probability says how confident to be.

facts.text: A statistic is a number describing a sample, such as its average; it estimates the matching number for the whole population, called a parameter.
How accurately a statistic estimates a parameter depends on how well the sample represents the population.
Inferential statistics uses probability to judge how confident we can be that conclusions drawn from a sample are correct.

title: Stir the pot, then taste a spoonful
description: A well-stirred pot lets one spoonful speak for the whole kettle; a well-mixed (random) sample lets a small sample speak for a population.

facts.text: A 1946 pamphlet on opinion polls compared sampling to a cook who stirs the broth thoroughly, then tastes one spoonful to test the whole kettle.

title: Random sampling: everyone gets the same chance
description: In a random sample every member of the population starts with the same chance of being picked; pollsters use random phone numbers or addresses to achieve it.

facts.text: In random sampling, each member of the population starts with an equal chance of being selected for the sample.
Gallup has a computer generate phone numbers at random, so unlisted numbers are as likely to be called as listed ones, giving every adult an equal chance.

title: Convenience samples and sampling bias
description: When some members are less likely to be chosen, the sample is biased; asking whoever is handy (a radio station polling its own concert crowd) tilts the result.

facts.text: Sampling bias arises when some members of a population are less likely to be chosen than others, and it can lead to wrong conclusions about the population.
In a textbook example, a radio station with 20,000 listeners asked the first 200 people it met at one of its music concerts; 176 wanted more music.

title: The 1969 draft lottery: a badly mixed draw
description: In the December 1969 US draft lottery, capsules went in month by month and were not mixed enough, so December birthdays drew disproportionately low numbers.

facts.text: In the December 1969 US draft lottery, 366 capsules, one for each day of the year, were drawn one at a time to set the order of the draft.
The capsules were put in the box month by month, January through December, and the mixing afterward was not enough to undo that order.
Men born in December drew disproportionately low numbers, meaning earlier calls, and statisticians charged that the lottery was not random.

title: The 1936 Literary Digest poll
description: The Literary Digest got about 2.4 million ballots back yet predicted Landon; Roosevelt won in a landslide. Its lists and its replies were both biased, while Gallup's smaller scientific sample called it.

facts.text: In 1936 the Literary Digest mailed about 10 million straw ballots and got about 2.4 million back.
The Digest predicted Alf Landon would beat President Franklin Roosevelt with about 57% of the vote; Roosevelt won in a landslide with more than 60%.
George Gallup, using a far smaller but systematic, scientific sample, predicted in 1936 that Roosevelt would win handily.
A 1988 study found the Digest's sample and its replies were both biased; had everyone polled replied, it would at least have picked Roosevelt to win.

title: The list you sample from, and why size can't fix bias
description: A sample can only include people on the list it is drawn from; the Digest's phone and car lists leaned well-off, and a bigger sample shrinks chance error but not bias.

facts.text: The Digest drew names from lists such as telephone owners and car registrations, which in the Great Depression leaned toward better-off Americans.
A larger sample shrinks sampling error, but a sample that doesn't represent the population is biased and gives inaccurate results however large.

title: Sample size doesn't depend on population size
description: The sample a poll needs depends on how precise it must be, not on how big the population is: about 1,000 can serve a town or a nation.

facts.text: The sample size needed depends on the precision wanted, not on population size: 1,000 can represent a population of 100,000 or of 1,000,000.
Pew's panel of about 10,000 adults, out of about 260 million US adults, gives each adult roughly a 1 in 26,000 chance of being in it.

title: Bigger samples help, then barely
description: The margin of error drops fast from 100 to 1,000 people, then slowly; about 1,000 random people give about plus or minus 3 points, and doubling to 2,000 buys about one point.

facts.text: A random sample of about 1,000 people gives a margin of error of about plus or minus 3 percentage points; 1,067 gives 3 points.
The margin of error falls steeply as samples grow from 100 to 1,000, then slowly: doubling from 1,000 to 2,000 cuts it by only about one point.

title: What a margin of error says
description: Plus or minus 3 at 95% confidence means about 95 of 100 repeats would land within 3 percentage points of the truth, and about 5 would not.

facts.text: A margin of plus or minus 3 points at 95% confidence means that if the survey were run 100 times, about 95 results would land within 3 points of the truth.
With a margin of plus or minus 3 points, a candidate polling at 48% could truly be anywhere from 45% to 51%.
About 5 times out of 100, a survey's result will fall outside its margin of error.
A margin of error is always expressed in percentage points, not as a percent: three percentage points, not 3%.

title: The margin on a lead is about double
description: If one candidate's share is too high by chance the other's is likely too low, so the margin on the gap is about double; a 5-point lead with plus or minus 3 could be -1 to +11.

facts.text: The margin on the gap between two candidates is about double, because if one's share is too high by chance, the other's is likely too low.
With plus or minus 3 for each candidate, a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11; it takes about 6 points to be confident.

title: What the margin of error leaves out
description: The margin counts only sampling error, not wording or nonresponse; it grows for small subgroups (about 160 people give about 8 points).

facts.text: The margin of error covers only sampling error; errors from question wording, people who don't respond or turnout guesses aren't in it.
Subgroups inside a poll have bigger margins: a group of about 160 people gets about plus or minus 8 points.

title: Nonresponse bias
description: When the people who skip a survey differ from those who answer in ways tied to its topic, the results skew; a low response rate alone doesn't make a poll wrong.

facts.text: If the people who answer a poll differ from those who don't on what it measures, nonresponse can bias the results, even when the sample was random.
The response rate of Pew's typical telephone survey fell from 36% in 1997 to 9% in 2012 and 6% in 2018.
Robocalls may be depressing response: poll calls look like one more unknown number, and phones and apps flag some survey calls as spam.
Pew studies in 1997, 2003, 2012 and 2016 found little link between response rates and accuracy; what matters is whether the topic is tied to who answers.
In 2012, 55% of Pew's phone respondents said they had volunteered in the past year, against 27% in the government's Current Population Survey.
The same motivation that leads people to volunteer seems to make them more willing to take surveys; volunteering isn't strongly tied to political views.

title: Weighting a sample to match the population
description: Pollsters give each answer a weight so the sample's mix of age, sex, race, education and region matches Census figures; underrepresented groups count more.

facts.text: Without adjustment, polls tend to overrepresent people who are easier to reach and underrepresent those who are harder to interview.
Gallup gives each respondent a weight so the sample's mix of gender, race, age, education and region matches the Census Bureau's latest estimates.
If young adults are 20% of a population but only 10% of a sample, each young adult's answers count about twice so the weighted mix matches.
Raking adjusts weights one trait after another until the sample matches known population figures; it's the standard method at Pew and many other pollsters.

title: What weighting can't fix
description: Weighting only balances the traits it uses; when answering is tied to the topic itself, as with volunteering, standard weighting falls short, and weighting widens the margin of error.

facts.text: Standard weighting corrects some nonresponse, but when polls measure volunteering it falls short, leaving the estimates biased.
Weighting is crucial for avoiding bias, but it also makes the margin of error larger, which statisticians call the design effect.

title: Wording changes the answer
description: Logically equal questions can get different answers: in 1941, 75% would 'not allow' speeches against democracy but only 54% would 'forbid' them. Split-ballot experiments reveal such effects.

facts.text: In a split-ballot experiment, a random half of the sample gets one wording and the other half gets another, so a difference comes from the wording.
In 1941, 75% of those answering said the US should 'not allow' public speeches against democracy, but only 54% said it should 'forbid' them.
One leading explanation is that 'forbid' sounds harsher than 'not allow', so fewer people are willing to say it.

title: Answer lists, order and agree-disagree questions
description: Offering an option makes more people choose it; people favor options by position, so pollsters shuffle them; agree-disagree questions tilt toward agreeing.

facts.text: When Pew offered the economy as a choice for the issue that mattered most to voters, 58% chose it; asked with no list, only 35% named it.
On the phone people more often pick options heard last, and on a screen options at the top, so Pew shuffles option order to spread that bias.
Some respondents tend to agree with whatever statement they're read; a better practice is to offer a choice between two statements.
Because small wording changes shift answers, comparing results over time requires the exact same question wording.

title: Self-selected (opt-in) polls
description: When people choose whether to take part, their chance of inclusion is unknown and the most interested answer, so no margin of error applies and the result speaks only for those who chose to answer.

facts.text: In self-selected, or opt-in, polls such as dial-in and many internet polls, people choose themselves; their chance of inclusion is unknown and results may not represent the population.
Pew won't base its polls on volunteers, who would likely be more politically interested and engaged than the average American.
A margin of error applies only when everyone has a known chance of being picked; it doesn't apply to opt-in online surveys.

title: Why online ratings form a J
description: Buyers with extreme opinions are likelier to review, so ratings pile up at 5 and 1 stars; when everyone rates, the ratings form a single hump.

facts.text: Online ratings often form a J: many 5 stars, some 1 star, few between, since buyers with extreme views are likelier to review to 'brag or moan'.
When researchers had every participant rate a product, the ratings formed a single hump, while the same product's Amazon ratings were J-shaped.
People with strong positive or negative opinions are the ones likely to answer voluntary surveys, which can skew the results.

title: Reading a poll's label
description: Trustworthy pollsters disclose who paid and who ran the poll, exact wording, the population, random or opt-in sample, size and margin, weighting and dates; judging a poll means checking them.

facts.text: AAPOR asks pollsters to disclose the sponsor, exact wording, population, whether the sample was random or opt-in, size and margin, weighting and dates.
Pew notes that pollsters who explain clearly and in detail how a poll was done tend to be more accurate than those who don't.

title: Watching vs. testing
description: An observational study records what people already do without changing who is exposed; an experiment changes something, such as who gets a treatment, and compares the results.

facts.text: In an observational study, researchers observe the effect of an exposure or treatment without trying to change who is or isn't exposed to it.
In an experiment, researchers introduce an intervention, changing something such as who gets a treatment, and measure its effects; experiments are usually randomized.

In a textbook example, people who regularly take vitamin E show better health on average, which doesn't prove vitamin E works: they often also exercise, eat well, take other supplements and don't smoke.
To show cause and effect, an experiment is designed so the only difference between the groups being compared is the planned treatment.

Some questions can only be studied by observation, because it would be unethical to deliberately expose people to something potentially harmful; observational results are open to dispute because of confounding.

title: James Lind's 1747 scurvy trial
description: On HMS Salisbury in 1747, James Lind gave six remedies to six pairs of similar scurvy patients kept on one diet; the citrus pair did best.

facts.text: On HMS Salisbury, naval surgeon James Lind began comparing six treatments then in use for scurvy in 12 sailors with the disease on 20 May 1747.
Lind reported that his 12 patients were "as similar as I could have them": they had the same symptoms, lay together in the same quarters and ate one diet common to all.
Lind gave two men each of six remedies: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water, two oranges and a lemon, or a medicinal paste.
The pair given oranges and lemons did best: one was fit for duty after six days, and the other recovered well enough to nurse the rest of the sick.
Historians credit Lind with taking care to "compare like with like", holding the patients' condition, surroundings and diet constant.

title: The control group
description: A control group gets no treatment or a dummy one, so the treatment's effect shows up as the difference between groups.

facts.text: A control group receives no treatment or an inactive placebo and is compared with the treated group; comparing the two shows whether changes come from the treatment or occur by chance.

title: Random assignment
description: Letting chance decide who gets the treatment spreads hidden differences evenly across the groups, so the only systematic difference left is the treatment.

facts.text: Lind never said how he decided which of his 12 patients received which of the six treatments.
When subjects are assigned to groups at random, the potential lurking variables are spread evenly among the groups, so the only difference left is the one the researcher imposed.
When researchers themselves choose who gets a treatment, the groups can differ in ways that bias the comparison; trial designers call this allocation or selection bias.
A fair coin lands heads with probability 0.5, so assigning volunteers by coin toss gives each one a 50% chance of either group.

title: The 1948 streptomycin trial
description: Britain's Medical Research Council used random numbers in sealed envelopes to decide which tuberculosis patients got streptomycin, a landmark randomized trial.

facts.text: In 1948 Britain's Medical Research Council reported a trial of the antibiotic streptomycin for tuberculosis of the lungs, with patients allocated using random numbers.

The allocation list was unknown to the investigators and kept in sealed envelopes, so no doctor could steer a patient into either group; the trial is often called the first randomized controlled trial in medicine.

title: Placebos
description: A placebo is an inactive look-alike of a treatment; giving it to a control group separates the treatment's effect from the effect of expecting to get better.

facts.text: The placebo effect is a beneficial health outcome that results from a person's expectation that a treatment will help.
A placebo is an inactive substance that looks like the drug or treatment being tested.
In a placebo-controlled trial, volunteers are randomly assigned to a group receiving the treatment or a control group receiving a placebo, and the two groups' results are compared.

title: Blinding
description: In a blind trial participants don't know which group they are in; in a double-blind trial the researchers working with them don't know either.

facts.text: In a blinded study, participants don't know who is getting the active treatment and who the placebo; in a double-blind study, neither do the researchers working with them.
In a textbook maze study, people could smell whether their mask was flower-scented, so they couldn't be blinded, but the researchers timing them could be.

title: Confounders: the hidden third factor
description: A confounder is something else that differs between the groups being compared and affects the result, making a comparison look like cause and effect.

facts.text: A study might find that people who meditate regularly get less heart disease, but the link may be explained by meditators also exercising more and eating healthier diets.
When the groups being compared also differ in other characteristics that affect the outcome, the comparison is confounded; such hidden factors are also called lurking variables.

title: Age-adjusted rates
description: Because age drives death rates, places with older people look worse on crude rates; an age-adjusted rate compares them as if they had the same mix of ages.

facts.text: Age is a prime factor in mortality, so counties with more older residents almost always have much higher crude death rates than counties with younger populations.
An age-adjusted rate combines the rates for each age group using the same standard mix of ages for every population, which reduces the confounding effect of age.

title: How strong is a link? The correlation
description: A correlation from -1 to +1 rates how closely the dots of a scatter plot follow a straight line: the sign gives direction, the size gives strength.

facts.text: In a textbook example, a shop owner records the noon temperature and ice cream cones sold on nine days; hotter days tend to bring more cones.
On a scatter plot, a positive correlation means that as one value increases the other tends to increase; a negative correlation means the other tends to decrease.
The correlation coefficient r is always between -1 and +1; values near -1 or +1 mean a strong straight-line link, and r near 0 means no straight-line link.
A correlation of exactly 1 or -1 means every point lies on a straight line, which real data almost never do.
A correlation only measures straight-line patterns: curved data can have a correlation of 0, and a strong correlation does not show that one thing causes the other.

title: Fisher's lady tasting tea
description: Fisher's 1935 tea test: 8 cups, 4 of each kind, in random order; guessing sorts them all correctly only 1 time in 70.

facts.text: In The Design of Experiments (1935), Ronald Fisher described testing a lady who said she could taste whether the milk or the tea was added to the cup first.
Fisher's test used 8 cups, 4 made each way, served in random order. There are 70 ways to pick 4 cups of 8, so pure guessing gets all right 1 time in 70 (about 1.4%).

title: What a p-value and "significant" mean
description: A p-value says how surprising results at least this striking would be if nothing were going on; results under a cutoff, often 5%, are called statistically significant. It is not the chance the finding is true.

facts.text: A p-value measures how incompatible the data are with a model in which nothing is going on: how surprising results at least this extreme would be if there were no real effect.
Fisher wrote that it is usual and convenient to take 5 percent (1 in 20) as a standard level of significance; results that fail to reach it are set aside.
The American Statistical Association warned in 2016 that a p-value does not measure the chance the hypothesis is true, or that the data came from chance alone: p = 0.05 is not a 5% chance of a fluke.

title: Significant isn't the same as big
description: Statistical significance doesn't measure how big or important an effect is; huge samples make tiny effects significant, so always ask for the effect size.

facts.text: The American Statistical Association's 2016 statement says a p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.
With a large enough sample, a test will almost always find a significant difference unless the effect is exactly zero; with 10,000 people, even a negligible difference is likely to be significant.
The effect size, how big the difference between groups actually is, is the main finding of a study; unlike significance, it does not depend on how many people took part.

title: Why one study is rarely enough
description: Even with no real effect, a 5% cutoff lets about 1 test in 20 come out significant, so a finding earns trust when repeats keep producing it.

facts.text: If there is no real effect, a test with a 5% significance cutoff will still come out significant about 5 times in 100 by chance alone.
Fisher wrote in 1935 that no isolated experiment, however significant, can prove a natural phenomenon; it is shown when we know an experiment that will rarely fail to give a significant result.
In the 2015 project, whether a result replicated was better predicted by the strength of the original evidence than by who ran the original or repeat studies.

title: The 2015 replication of 100 psychology studies
description: The Open Science Collaboration repeated 100 published psychology studies: 97% of originals were significant, only 36% of repeats, with effects about half as big.

facts.text: In a project published in Science in 2015, the Open Science Collaboration repeated 100 experimental and correlational studies from three psychology journals.
97% of the original studies had statistically significant results, but only 36% of the replications did, and replication effects were on average half the size of the originals.

title: The ladder of evidence
description: Evidence is often ranked: systematic reviews at the top, then randomized controlled trials, then observational cohort and case-control studies.

facts.text: In the widely accepted hierarchy of evidence, the most reliable evidence comes from systematic reviews, then randomized controlled trials, then cohort studies and then case-control studies.
The randomized, placebo-controlled trial is often called the "gold standard" for testing treatments in people.
Besides his trial, Lind searched for, summarized and evaluated earlier reports on scurvy: in effect, a systematic review of what others had written.

title: Read a chart's words before its shape
description: Before judging a chart's shape, read its title and subtitle (what, where, when), its axis titles (units) and its source.

facts.text: Official UK chart guidance says a chart's title should state its main message, and its subtitle should give what was measured, where, and over what time period.
UK government chart guidance gives "Number of people living in one person households, England, 1991 to 2021" as an example subtitle: what, where and when.
Axis titles should give the unit of measurement shown on each axis, and every axis should be clearly labelled.
Every chart should name the specific source of its data, so readers can find it, not just point to an organization in general.

title: The chopped-off axis
description: A bar chart's axis should start at zero because bars are judged by length; cutting it off, Huff's 1954 gee-whiz graph, makes small gaps look huge.

facts.text: In How to Lie with Statistics (1954), Darrell Huff chopped the bottom off a graph of national income rising 10% in a year, so the line climbed halfway up the page; he called it the gee-whiz graph.
A bar chart's axis should start at zero: readers judge bars by their lengths, and starting the axis higher distorts their proportions.
Bars of 50 and 52 differ by 4% (2 ÷ 50 = 0.04), but on an axis starting at 48 they are drawn 2 and 4 units tall, so one looks twice the other.
Line charts may start their axis above zero when values sit in a narrow range, as long as the break is made clear; bar chart axes should not be broken.

title: Picking the start date
description: Where a chart starts and ends is a choice, and cherry-picking the window can turn the same data into a rise or a fall.

facts.text: The Royal Statistical Society warns that cherry-picking points in time can mislead, for example by picking unrepresentative time points or too short a time frame.
A price going from 100 to a peak of 150 and ending at 120 is up 20% from the start (20 ÷ 100 = 0.2) but down 20% from the peak (30 ÷ 150 = 0.2).
UK statistics regulator guidance says quoting only the most recent figure in a time series can mislead if it isn't representative of the wider trend.

title: Maps that show where people live
description: Maps shaded by totals mostly show where people live; dividing by population (normalizing) maps a rate that compares places fairly.

facts.text: A 2012 xkcd comic, 'Heatmap', showed three US maps of different groups of people looking nearly identical, because each was basically a map of where people live.
Mapping raw counts about people, rather than rates, mostly highlights population centers; a Penn State mapping course calls this population dependence.
Normalizing divides each area's count by its population to map a rate, such as cases per 100,000 people, so large and small areas compare fairly.

title: A pie is one whole
description: A pie chart's circle stands for the whole, so its slices must add up to 100%; multi-answer surveys and 3D tilts break pies.

facts.text: A pie chart's circle stands for the whole, 100%, so its slices should add up to 100%.
Survey questions where people can pick more than one answer, like favorite pizza toppings, can total more than 100%, so they do not belong in a pie chart.
3D pie charts distort the apparent size of slices: slices nearer the viewer look bigger than they are.

title: Pictures that grow two ways at once
description: A picture drawn twice as tall is also twice as wide, so it covers four times the area and exaggerates the difference.

facts.text: Huff (1954) showed that a moneybag drawn twice as tall to show $60 against $30 is also twice as wide, covering four times the area; as a solid it suggests eight times the money, $240.
The Royal Statistical Society warns that icon charts can mislead because comparing areas is harder than comparing heights.

title: Two axes, one story
description: A chart with a separate scale on each side lets its maker place the lines anywhere, so crossings mean little; guidance says use two charts.

facts.text: UK government chart guidance says dual-axis charts are easily misinterpreted and can be manipulated to show almost any relationship, and recommends separate charts with their own axes.

In the guidance's example, the UK employment rate for people aged 16 to 64 (above 70%) and the unemployment rate (under 10%), 2009 to 2022, share a dual-axis chart, and a reader might conclude unemployment exceeded employment from 2009 to 2015.

title: Log scales
description: On a log scale each step up multiplies, so huge ranges fit on one chart and steady exponential growth looks like a straight line; many readers misread them.

facts.text: On a log scale, the distance from 1 to 10 is the same as from 10 to 100, or from 100,000 to 1,000,000: each equal step multiplies by the same amount.
A thousand, a million and a billion sit at equal steps on a log axis, because each is 1,000 times the one before.
Something growing at a steady rate, such as doubling every so often, curves ever more steeply upward on an ordinary axis but makes a straight line on a log axis.
Gordon Moore drew his 1965 graph of transistor counts on computer chips on a logarithmic scale; the count has doubled roughly every two years.
In a 2020 experiment with about 2,000 US residents, about 41% of people shown COVID-19 deaths on a log scale answered a basic question correctly, against about 84% shown a linear scale.

title: Running totals always go up
description: A cumulative chart adds every new count to a running total, so it never falls; slowing shows only as a flatter bend.

facts.text: A cumulative chart shows a running total, so when counts cannot be negative it never goes down: it rises when new cases arrive and stays flat when none do.
When the number of new cases each period is falling, the cumulative curve still rises but bends flatter; a flat line means no new cases.
Weekly counts of 100, 80, 60 and 40 give running totals of 100, 180, 240 and 280: the total keeps climbing while each week is lower than the last.
The Math Doctors advise checking a chart's axis labels and description to tell a cumulative total from current numbers, since a cumulative graph will never go down.

title: Error bars
description: Error bars draw a range of uncertainty around an estimate, not a size; a chart should say what kind of range they show.

facts.text: The Royal Statistical Society suggests giving a range, such as between 190 and 210 rather than just 200, and showing uncertainty with error bars or shaded areas.
Error bars can show different things, such as confidence intervals, standard errors or standard deviations, so a figure must say what its error bars represent.

title: The hurricane cone
description: The National Hurricane Center's cone shows the probable track of a storm's center, sized from past errors; the center strays outside about one time in three, and effects reach far beyond it.

facts.text: The National Hurricane Center's forecast cone shows the probable track of a storm's center; its circles are sized so two-thirds of past official forecast errors fall inside, and they grow larger for later forecast times.
Because the cone holds two-thirds of past errors, a storm's center can be expected to stray outside it about one time in three.
The cone does not show a storm's size: a tropical cyclone's effects can span hundreds of miles from the center and reach well beyond the cone.

title: Retelling a chart fairly in words
description: Take a chart apart in order (words, scales, choices) and restate its story in one sentence with the real numbers.

facts.text: UK government chart guidance notes that a well-structured table can often be as powerful as a chart.

title: Simpson's paradox and the Berkeley admissions data
description: A trend in every group can reverse when groups are combined, as when Berkeley's 1973 overall admission rates favored men while most large departments admitted women at higher rates.

facts.text: In Simpson's paradox, a trend that appears in several groups of data disappears or reverses when the groups are combined.
In fall 1973, UC Berkeley's graduate programs admitted about 44% of the 8,442 men who applied and about 35% of the 4,321 women.
