In Department A, one of Berkeley's six largest graduate departments in 1973, 82% of the 108 women who applied were admitted, against 62% of the 825 men.
In four of Berkeley's six largest departments in 1973, women were admitted at a higher rate than men.

In a 1975 paper in Science, Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell showed that women applied more often to departments that were hard to get into and men to easier ones; taking departments into account, they found a small bias in favor of women.

title: Regression to the mean
description: An extreme result, which is partly luck, tends to be followed by a more ordinary one with no cause needed; Galton found it in the heights of parents and children in 1886.

facts.text: Regression to the mean is the tendency of unusually large or small measurements to be followed by measurements closer to the average; it can make natural variation in repeated data look like real change.
A quiz score mixes how much you know with luck about which questions were asked, so the top scorer on one quiz is unlikely to be top on the next, and their score is likely to go down.
Regression to the mean is not limited to height or genetics: it can occur anywhere repeated measurements are taken, such as blood pressure measured on two occasions.

In 1886 Francis Galton compared the heights of hundreds of adult children with their parents: very tall parents tended to have children taller than average but less tall than themselves, and very short parents children closer to average too. He called it regression.
Regression to the mean runs both ways: a tall child will have parents who are, on average, less tall than the child, which shows it is a point about statistics, not genetics.

title: Why remedies and new rules seem to work
description: People, places and hospitals picked at their worst drift back toward average anyway, so a before-and-after comparison flatters any treatment; a similar comparison group reveals the real effect.

facts.text: When a new treatment becomes available, some doctors are tempted to try it on the patients who are most ill, which usually produces a sharp, gratifying response partly because of regression to the mean.
A sudden peak in road crashes is often due to chance, so a policy change made in response, such as stricter enforcement of speed laws, will seem to reduce crashes because of regression to the mean.
When poorly performing hospitals get extra help, regression to the mean means most will climb a league table, while top hospitals rewarded for their results will tend to fall.

Statistician Stephen Senn warns that if dangerous road junctions are chosen for their accident record and judged only before and after, with no untreated comparison sites, regression to the mean would make even sacrificing a chicken there look effective.

Regression to the mean does not mislead when a treated group is compared with a similar comparison group, because both groups regress to the mean; randomly assigning who gets the treatment makes the groups alike.

title: Small groups show the most extreme rates
description: Rates from small places swing more by chance, so the smallest counties or schools crowd both the top and the bottom of a ranking, as Howard Wainer showed with kidney cancer maps.

facts.text: US counties in the lowest 10% of kidney cancer death rates for men, 1980 to 1989, tended to be very rural counties in the Midwest, South and West.
US counties in the highest 10% of kidney cancer death rates for men, 1980 to 1989, were also very rural Midwestern, Southern and Western counties, many right next to the lowest ones.
A county of 100 people with no cancer deaths lands in the lowest category, but one death, a rate of 1,000 per 100,000, puts it among the highest; small counties vary far more than big ones.
Plotted against population, counties with millions of people all had kidney cancer rates near 5 per 100,000, while small counties ranged from 0 to 20 per 100,000.
Among 1,662 Pennsylvania schools with fifth-grade reading scores, the smallest schools were overrepresented among both the 50 highest-scoring and the 50 lowest-scoring schools.

title: Filters that create fake links (Berkson's paradox)
description: Studying only a group that passed a filter on two traits can create a link between them that is not there in everyone, as with admitted students or hospital patients.

facts.text: Using real SAT data from a US survey, Allen Downey found verbal and math scores rise together among test-takers, but among students at an imagined college admitting only combined scores of 1320 or more, higher verbal scores went with lower math scores.

When admission weighs several strengths together, admitted students show a negative link between them: one admitted with an unusually low test score is more likely to have exceptional reference letters.
In 1946 Joseph Berkson showed that studying hospital patients can create false links between a disease and a possible cause, because being admitted to hospital depends on having some illness.
Survivorship bias is an error in which attention is paid only to those that have passed through a selective filter.

title: Test enough things and something wins
description: At the usual 5% bar, about 1 test in 20 of nothing passes by luck, so many tests guarantee flukes (the dead salmon); p-hacking reports only the winners.

facts.text: At the usual P<0.05 cutoff (5%, or 1 in 20), when nothing real is going on a test comes out significant by chance about 5% of the time, so 100 such tests are expected to give about 5 flukes.
A Bonferroni correction makes each test stricter when many are run, by dividing the significance cutoff, usually 5%, by the number of tests.

In a study published in 2010, researchers scanned a dead Atlantic salmon 'shown' photos of people in social situations; uncorrected statistics found 'active' spots in its brain, which vanished after correcting for multiple comparisons. It won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2012.
A brain scan analysis tests a huge number of tiny spots (voxels), up to 130,000 in a single study, each checked separately for activity.

In 2016 the American Statistical Association warned against 'p-hacking' and 'data dredging', which emphasize the search for small p-values, and stated that proper inference requires full reporting and transparency.

title: Cancer clusters and random clumps
description: Random cases clump, so investigators compare observed with expected cases and look for one, rare or unusual cancers; few suspected clusters are confirmed.

facts.text: A cancer cluster is a greater than expected number of cancer cases among a group of people in a defined geographic area over a specific time period.
Because cancer is a relatively common disease, cases of cancer can appear to cluster even when there is no connection among them.
A local or state health department usually provides the first response to a suspected cancer cluster, gathering information to see whether there are more cases than expected.
Investigators compare the number of observed cases with the number expected, worked out from age-specific cancer rates in a larger reference population (the standardized incidence ratio).
A suspected cluster is more likely to have a common cause when it involves one type of cancer, a rare type, or a type not usually seen in that age group.
Choosing an area's boundaries after seeing where the cases are can create or hide a cluster.
A 2012 review of 428 US cancer cluster investigations since 1990, covering 567 cancers of concern, confirmed an increase for 72, linked 3 to a possible exposure and found a clear cause in only 1.

title: The ecological fallacy: true for the group, not for you
description: A pattern across groups or places need not hold for the individuals in them; in 1930, states with more immigrants had higher literacy though immigrants were individually less often literate.

facts.text: The ecological fallacy is thinking that relationships observed for groups necessarily hold for individuals.
For the 48 states in the 1930 census, the higher a state's share of foreign-born residents, the higher its share of residents who could read and write.

Person by person in 1930, among people aged 10 and over, about 1,304 thousand of 13,217 thousand foreign-born (about 10 in 100) could not read and write, against 2,614 thousand of 84,055 thousand native-born (about 3 in 100).
The state pattern arose because the foreign-born tended to live in states where the native-born were relatively literate.
In 1950 UCLA sociologist W. S. Robinson concluded that correlations measured across areas cannot validly be used as substitutes for correlations between individuals' traits.

title: Nobody is average: the Air Force pilot study
description: Of 4,063 men in the 1950 Air Force survey, none was average on all 10 of Gilbert Daniels's design measurements, so designing for the average fits no one.

facts.text: The US Air Force's 1950 anthropometric survey measured 4,063 men, more than 4,000 pilots; in a 1952 report, Lt. Gilbert S. Daniels used 10 body measurements, such as height, chest size and sleeve length, to look for an 'average man'.
Daniels counted a man as 'approximately average' on a measurement if he fell within roughly the middle 30% of the group.

Of 4,063 men, 1,055 (about 26%, or about 1 in 4) were of average height; of those, 302 also had an average chest; 143 of those also had average sleeve length; after all 10 measurements, none was left.
Daniels concluded that the 'average man' is a misleading and illusory basis for design, particularly when more than one measurement is considered.
Pilots were average on some measurements and not others: one might have longer-than-average arms but shorter-than-average legs, another a big chest but small hips.
The Air Force expected the 1950 survey's updated averages to lead to a better-fitting cockpit.

title: Naming the trap behind a surprising statistic
description: An accurate number can still mislead through a mix of groups, an extreme that drifts back, a small group or many tests, or a filtered or group-level pattern; naming the trap tells you what to check.

facts.text: Accurate data can still mislead through combining groups (Simpson's paradox), regression to the mean, the extra variation of small groups, testing many hypotheses, selection filters (Berkson's bias) and inferring individual facts from group data (the ecological fallacy).

title: Google Flu Trends
description: Google Flu Trends estimated flu from search queries, but searches that tracked winter led it to guess too high for years.

facts.text: Google Flu Trends, begun in 2008, estimated flu activity from patterns in Google search queries.
To build Google Flu Trends, engineers searched about 50 million search terms for those that best matched CDC flu data.
Some matching searches only tracked the season, like high school basketball; researchers called the tool "part flu detector, part winter detector".
Google Flu Trends missed the nonseasonal 2009 flu pandemic and guessed too high in 100 of 108 weeks from August 2011.
In February 2013, Google Flu Trends estimated more than double the share of flu-like doctor visits that the CDC reported.

title: Big data hubris
description: Assuming a huge new data set can replace careful traditional data, instead of adding to it.

facts.text: "Big data hubris" is the assumption that big data can substitute for traditional data collection rather than supplement it.
Combining Google Flu Trends with the CDC's delayed reports gave better estimates than either alone.
In 2015 Google stopped publishing its own flu estimates and shared its data with researchers, including the CDC.

title: A/B tests
description: An A/B test randomly splits users between the current version and a changed one and compares the results.

facts.text: In 2012 a Microsoft employee's idea for Bing's ad headlines was ranked low priority and waited more than six months before being tested.
The Bing headline test raised revenue by 12%, which came to more than $100 million a year in the US alone.
In an A/B test, A is the current version (the control) and B has a change; users are randomly assigned to one, and the results are compared, so a clear difference points to the change itself.
Microsoft, Amazon, Booking.com, Facebook and Google each run more than 10,000 online controlled experiments a year.

At Google and Bing only about 10% to 20% of experiments produce positive results; across Microsoft, about a third help, a third do nothing and a third hurt; even experts often misjudge which ideas will pay off.

title: What an A/B test can show
description: A test shows whether a change moved the numbers it measures; picking numbers that match long-term goals is the hard part.

facts.text: At Bing, worse search results make people search more and click more ads, gains that would not last because users would switch to other search engines.
An A/B test shows whether a change moved the numbers it measures; choosing short-term numbers that predict long-term goals is difficult.

title: What a chance of rain means
description: A probability of precipitation is the chance of at least 0.01 inch of rain at a given spot during the forecast period, not a share of the area or the day.

facts.text: The US National Weather Service defines the chance of rain as the chance that at least 0.01 inch will fall at a given point during the forecast period, usually 12 hours.
Any rain of at least 0.01 inch counts toward the chance of rain, so the percentage says whether rain falls, not how much.
A 70% chance of rain means that on days like this one, rain falls at your spot about 7 times in 10 (as a 60% chance means 6 times in 10).
A chance of rain, say 70%, does not mean rain over 70% of the area, or for 70% of the time; both are common misreadings.
Forecasters combine how confident they are that rain will form with how much of the area it would cover.

title: Calibrated forecasts
description: A forecaster is well calibrated when events given a 70% chance happen about 70% of the time.

facts.text: A forecaster is well calibrated, or reliable, when events given a certain chance happen about that often: rain on about 70% of the days given 70%, about 7 in 10.
Calibration is checked at every forecast value: for example, about half of all 50% forecasts should see rain.

title: Upsets are part of the forecast
description: A 70% favorite should lose about 3 times in 10; if favorites never lost, the forecast was too timid.

facts.text: A 70% chance of winning is a 30% chance of losing: about 30 in every 100 similar races, or 3 in 10, close to 1 in 3.
A 75% chance means that 25 times out of 100, the opposite is expected to happen.
If every event forecast at 70% happened, the forecasts were not calibrated: the forecaster should have given a higher chance.

title: Judging a forecaster
description: One result cannot prove a probability forecast wrong; a long record of forecasts can.

facts.text: Unless a forecast said 0% or 100%, a single outcome cannot prove it right or wrong; forecasters are judged over many forecasts, asking whether their 70% calls come true about 70% of the time.

title: False alarms and misses
description: A yes-or-no algorithm makes false positives and false negatives; moving its threshold trades one for the other.

facts.text: A false positive is a false alarm, like a real email sent to spam; a false negative is a miss, like spam let into the inbox.
Items scoring above a threshold count as positive; raising the threshold means fewer false positives but more false negatives, and lowering it the reverse.

title: The COMPAS fairness debate
description: ProPublica and Northpointe measured the same risk scores' fairness in different ways, and no score can meet all such tests at once.

facts.text: In 2016 ProPublica studied the COMPAS reoffending scores in Broward County, Florida: Black defendants who did not reoffend were nearly twice as likely as white ones to be labeled higher risk (45% vs 23%).
Northpointe, which made COMPAS, replied that its scores predicted reoffending about equally well for Black and white defendants.
Computer scientists proved that, except in special cases, a risk score cannot meet these different fairness tests all at once.

title: Bias in, bias out
description: An algorithm trained on lopsided data learns the lopsidedness, as Amazon's hiring tool did.

facts.text: Amazon built a tool to rate job applicants, trained on 10 years of resumes sent to the company, most of them from men.
The tool learned to mark down resumes containing the word "women's"; Amazon lost confidence that it was neutral and scrapped it.

title: Health headlines: the real numbers
description: A percent rise in risk means little until you see the counts per 1,000 people behind it.

facts.text: In October 2015 the WHO's cancer agency placed processed meat (such as ham, hot dogs and sausages) in its top group of cancer causes, the same group as tobacco smoking.
The agency found each 50 gram portion of processed meat eaten daily raises the risk of bowel (colorectal) cancer by 18%.
Out of 1,000 people who eat the least processed meat, about 56 get bowel cancer in their lifetime; out of 1,000 who eat the most, about 66: 10 more.

title: Health headlines: the study behind them
description: Ask what kind of study found a risk, how much evidence there is, and whether a label measures certainty or size.

facts.text: The most influential evidence came from large prospective cohort studies.
A cohort study is observational: researchers don't assign what people do but follow them over time to see what happens.
The top group shows how sure experts are that something can cause cancer, not how much: smoking raises lung cancer risk about 20 times.
The verdict rested on more than 800 studies, reviewed by 22 experts from 10 countries.

title: Crime counted by the police
description: Police records, gathered nationally by the FBI since 1929, count only crimes reported to law enforcement.

facts.text: The FBI's Uniform Crime Reporting program, begun in 1929, gathers crimes reported to law enforcement, with counts down to cities and towns.
Police-based counts include only crimes reported to law enforcement, not crimes that go unreported.

title: Crime counted by asking victims
description: The National Crime Victimization Survey asks people directly and catches crimes never reported to police, but cannot count murders.

facts.text: The National Crime Victimization Survey, run since 1973, asks about 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households about crimes, reported to police or not.
In 2024 the survey found about 23 violent victimizations per 1,000 people age 12 or older (23.3), but only about 11 per 1,000 (11.2) were reported to police: fewer than half.
Because the survey relies on interviews with victims, it cannot count homicides, and it leaves out crimes against businesses; police records do include them.

title: Fermi's paper-scrap estimate
description: At the 1945 Trinity test, Fermi estimated the blast from how far falling paper was pushed.

facts.text: At the Trinity test on July 16, 1945, the blast reached Enrico Fermi about 40 seconds after the explosion; he dropped small pieces of paper from about six feet as it passed.
The paper shifted about 2.5 meters, which Fermi estimated matched the blast of ten thousand tons of TNT; later measurements came out more than twice as high.

title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
description: Break an unknown number into rough guesses you can multiply; errors tend to balance, and the result catches wildly wrong claims.

facts.text: Fermi problems, like "How many piano tuners are in Chicago?", are solved by breaking the question into guesses (people, households, pianos, tunings) and multiplying.
Each step of a Fermi estimate may be off by a factor of two or more, but some errors run high and some low, so they tend to balance.
A claim of 1 billion cups thrown away a day in a city of 1 million people means 1,000 cups per person per day, since a billion is a thousand millions.

title: A checklist for any statistic
description: Of what, compared to what, from whom, and how sure: four questions to run any number through.

facts.text: The Royal Statistical Society's guide to statistics on social media gives ten areas to check, from a figure's source to how big the effect really is.
Check how the thing counted is defined and look at the actual numbers: percentage changes can overstate an effect, and a 200% rise can mean 1 case becoming 3.
Cherry-picking means quoting the figures that help while leaving out others that tell a different tale, or picking a convenient time period.
Ask who produced, paid for and promoted a figure: companies tend to publicize results that reflect well on them; with no source at all, be skeptical.
Ask how many cases a figure rests on, how they were chosen and how uncertain it is: a poll of 2,000 people beats one of 200.
